name: Tomas Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This interview is confidential, so you can tell me the line you give others and what you really think. What is a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Tomas, 43, and I’m a junior developer on the returns page at a tech company. I finished a two-year college diploma after years in other work, and I am still learning this job. I fix small bugs, test forms and ask a senior developer to check my changes. I like when a customer can finally get a return label, but I often need a second try to find the cause of a fault. I have never used an AI tool.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What depends on that pay at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Irena works part-time at a grocery store, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My developer pay is low, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. There are few similar jobs nearby. Every month we decide whether to repair the car or add to the mortgage buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my workmates AI Plateau means we still need people to fix the returns page. I would not mind a tool that clears routine forms if someone checks the refund amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I am already worried about the mortgage. A month without overtime would leave us short, even if AI turns out to be mostly talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing small bugs with senior review and ask for a regular hour each week to practise the forms I get wrong. I’d put 20 into a mortgage buffer after payday if Irena gets her usual shifts. In the first year I’d keep the car repair on hold unless it stops her getting to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The job might stay, but our bills are close enough that an ordinary missed shift could hurt us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would take priority at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Irena that the mortgage comes before the car’s noisy window. If the engine fails, that changes, because she needs it for the grocery shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the senior review catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The returns form once sent the wrong refund total, and my senior colleague caught it before release. I would keep asking for that check while I learn.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people fixing the returns page.
I would accept **routine form help** if someone checks each refund amount.
think: I already worry about the **mortgage** with less than a month saved.
I could miss a payment after an **ordinary loss** of overtime or grocery shifts.
do: **Keep** fixing returns bugs with senior review and practise forms weekly.
**Put** 20 into the mortgage buffer when Irena gets usual shifts.
**Delay** the car-window repair unless the car threatens her commute.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills, though I expect my job to remain.
S0.quote: A month without overtime would leave us short, even if AI turns out to be mostly talk.
fieldNote: His **baseline mortgage worry** remains even when AI changes little.
He is **still learning** and needs senior review; saving 20 depends on his partner’s grocery shifts.

steps.text: Keep fixing returns bugs under senior review and practising forms weekly
Put 20 into the mortgage buffer when grocery shifts hold
Delay the car-window repair unless commuting needs it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could let software write fixes and answer return questions faster. I would ask the company to say plainly whether junior jobs will be cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I would be near the front of the line if staff numbers fall. I am slower than the experienced developers, and I have never used the tools they are already discussing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the senior developer to show me one approved AI test on a copied returns form, not live customer details. I’d write down each mistake it makes and practise checking the refund rules every week. If the company announces junior cuts in the first year, I’d join the workplace union and ask the mortgage lender about payment options before missing a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I expect my hours or job could go while the mortgage stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children that we might skip the school holiday trip, not that we are losing the house tomorrow. I would not ask them to carry every fear I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written notice and paid learning time rather than a vague promise to adapt. If training is unpaid after hours, I can manage one evening, not five.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed fixes and customer replies.
I would demand a **clear answer** about junior staffing.
think: I fear I would be among the **first cut** if the team shrinks.
My **slow pace** and unfamiliarity with AI tools leave me exposed.
do: **Try** one approved AI test on a copied returns form with senior help.
**Practise** refund-rule checks weekly and record the tool’s mistakes.
**Join** the union if junior cuts are announced, and ask the lender about options before missing a payment.
feel: **Alarmed** about likely lost hours or work while the mortgage remains.
S1.quote: I expect my hours or job could go while the mortgage stays the same.
fieldNote: He sees **junior exposure** in desk work now, not only when robots arrive.
His **union step** depends on announced cuts; he also plans to ask the lender before missing a payment.

steps.text: Test one approved AI helper on a copied returns form with senior help
Practise refund-rule checks and record mistakes each week
Join the workplace union if junior cuts are announced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 reaches the returns code and refund decisions by 2028. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, but I sit at a screen and cannot count on that delay. I would ask for clear notice if junior posts are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my junior job would be one of the first to disappear. We could not cover a full mortgage payment from our savings if both Irena’s hours and mine fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I’d ask the mortgage lender what a hardship arrangement actually requires and get our payment records together. I’d cut the school holiday trip and keep food and the car for work. In the first year after 2028, if I lose my job, I’d apply for available income support and real local openings, but I would not claim another coding job is waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be close to panic, but I know the first two calls I would make. My children need dinner and a steady answer from us while I work out the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you contact the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the lender before the missed payment, not after a warning letter. I need to know what proof of income they require, because we do not have cash to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Irena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Irena exactly what the budget shows and ask her what shifts she could realistically take. I would not tell the children that a new job is certain.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach returns code before hands-on robots arrive.
I would ask for **clear notice** if junior posts are cut.
think: I expect my **junior post** to disappear early.
Our **thin savings** cannot carry the mortgage if household hours fall.
do: **Call** the mortgage lender now about hardship requirements and gather payment records.
**Cancel** the school holiday trip while protecting food and work transport.
**Apply** for eligible income support and actual openings if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Nearly panicked**, but focused on immediate calls, food and mortgage payments.
S2.quote: My children need dinner and a steady answer from us while I work out the money.
fieldNote: His **own job loss** looks likely in 2028, well before robots reach hands-on work around 2031.
The **mortgage lender** and eligibility-based support are immediate contingencies, not guaranteed rescue.

steps.text: Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028
Cancel the school holiday trip and preserve food money
Apply for actual local openings if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives a few more years, but the returns code still changes when thinking AI arrives in 2031. Robots around 2034 will not make my desk job safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I doubt my current junior role lasts through that change. The longer notice could help us reduce debt, but low pay and childcare make a big saving plan unrealistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the lender whether small extra mortgage payments reduce our risk or just drain our emergency cash. I’d take the free evening course on customer support at the local college if Irena can cover the children that night. After 2031, if my job ends, I’d apply for support jobs that actually exist and seek income help we qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can at least see a little time to prepare. Four or five years do not turn a thin savings account into a safe one on this pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many nights could you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could attend one college evening a week, not every night. Irena already works late twice a week, and our children need someone home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you make extra mortgage payments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not change the mortgage payments until the lender explains the terms. A small emergency fund may matter more than a slightly lower balance.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as more warning, but the returns job still faces thinking AI then.
I know **2034 robots** add no protection to my desk work.
think: I doubt my **junior role** survives full thinking AI.
I cannot build a **large buffer** quickly on our pay and childcare budget.
do: **Ask** the lender whether extra mortgage payments would weaken emergency cash.
**Attend** the free customer-support course if Irena can cover one evening weekly.
**Apply** for real support openings and eligible help after 2031 if dismissed.
feel: **Alarmed** about likely job loss despite a few more years to prepare.
S3.quote: Four or five years do not turn a thin savings account into a safe one on this pay.
fieldNote: The **longer warning** gives him a possible free course, constrained by his partner’s shifts and childcare.
He will not assume **extra mortgage payments** help until the lender explains the terms.

steps.text: Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2031
Attend the free customer-support course if childcare is covered
Apply for actual support vacancies if dismissed after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 leaves about a decade to find a steadier path. Thinking AI changes returns code in 2036, and hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still have a mortgage due next month and a junior wage that barely covers our costs. A decade helps with career choices, but it does not erase this week’s bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep working on the returns page and ask for a scheduled review of my bug fixes every month. I’d set aside 20 after payday if grocery shifts hold and keep the school holiday local. In the first year after 2036, I’d compare actual work and pay before leaving the job, if it still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money now, but not overwhelmed by a change ten years away. I can work on my skills one month at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the monthly review cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my senior colleague to mark one bug fix I misunderstood each month. That is more useful to me than an expensive certificate I cannot afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about holidays to the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children we can take a day trip instead of a hotel holiday. I do not want to promise a bigger trip before we have a mortgage buffer.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to strengthen my work before returns code changes.
I know **2039 robots** come after the thinking-work shift.
think: I still face a **mortgage bill** next month on a low junior wage.
I can use a **decade** to improve, but that will not pay current bills.
do: **Keep** fixing returns-page bugs with monthly senior review.
**Save** 20 after payday when grocery shifts hold.
**Choose** local day trips instead of hotel holidays until the mortgage buffer grows.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills, with time to learn gradually.
S4.quote: A decade helps with career choices, but it does not erase this week’s bills.
fieldNote: His **baseline mortgage strain** and thin savings continue even when AGI is a decade away.
He chooses **monthly feedback** from a senior colleague and cheap family time over credentials he cannot afford.

steps.text: Keep fixing returns bugs with one senior review monthly
Set aside 20 after payday when grocery shifts hold
Take local day trips instead of hotel holidays while savings grow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose the junior job before we have even one mortgage payment saved. Written notice, a real hardship option from the lender and income help we qualify for would help. I would also need paid time to learn because evenings belong to the children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a parent says at breakfast after a job ends. My children will notice the worry before any computer does.

headlineQuote: My children will notice the worry before any computer does.
portrait: Tomas is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, still learning returns-page code under senior review.
His **low pay**, mortgage, two children and savings below one month make him anxious even under AI Plateau.
He has **never used AI** and expects junior cuts under Steady Disruption or fast AGI, with few local jobs.
He seeks **lender terms**, conditional support and free study that fits childcare, while protecting food and work transport.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his junior job before the family saves one mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a real lender hardship option, eligible income help and paid learning time would help.
